VOLUME ESTIMATES FOR ALEXANDROV SPACES WITH
CONVEX BOUNDARIES
JIAN GE
Abstract. In this note, we estimate the upper bound of volume of
closed positively or nonnegatively curved Alexandrov space X with
strictly convex boundary. We also discuss the equality case. In par-
ticular, the Boundary Conjecture holds when the volume upper bound
is achieved. Our theorem also can be applied to Riemannian manifolds
with non-smooth boundary, which generalizes Heintze and Karcher’s
classical volume comparison theorem.
Our main tool is the gradient
ﬂow of semi-concave functions.
0. Introduction
Let (Mn, g) be a smooth Riemannian manifold and N m ⊂M be a sub-
manifold. In [HK78], Heintze and Karcher developed a general comparison
theorem for N-Jacobi ﬁelds normal to the submanifold N. As an application,
they were able to estimate the volume of a tube around the submanifold N
in terms of the lower curvature bound of M and upper bound of the norm
of mean curvature vectors of N etc. But the technique does not apply if
the embedding N →M is not smooth. For example the boundary of the
Alexandrov Lens Sn−2 ∗[0, α] deﬁned in [GMP], with its intrinsic length dis-
tance, is a perfectly round sphere Sn−1, but the embedding is non-smooth.
To address this kind of problem, we meet non-smooth spaces inevitably.
Alexandrov spaces can be viewed as a generalization of Riemannian man-
ifolds under lower sectional curvature bound, but with some singularities.
Since the spaces that we are interested in are non-smooth in nature, we
cannot expect to estimate the whole tube around N without addressing the
geometry of the singularities of the embedding N →M. Nevertheless, we
are able to estimate the one-side neighborhood of a convex hypersurface. We
use [BBI01], [BGP92] and [Pet07] as our references for Alexandrov spaces.
We use Alexn(κ) to denote the set of all n-dimensional Alexandrov spaces
with lower curvature bound: curv ≥κ. For X ∈Alexn(κ) with ∂X ̸= ∅, the
boundary ∂X is geodesically convex by the very deﬁnition of Alexandrov
spaces.
We need the following deﬁnition from Alexander and Bishop to
measure the convexity of ∂X ⊂X quantitatively at footpoints. Recall that
p ∈∂X is called a footpoint, if p is the endpoint of a shortest geodesic from a

Since we are interested in the volume estimates, the boundary ∂X is
assumed to be compact, even though many of our estimates hold locally.
We always assume ∂X is equipped with the length metric induced from X.
It is still a conjecture that ∂X itself is an Alexandrov space with the same
lower curvature bound as of that of X. See the recent development of this
conjecture in [GMP].

Next, we study the concavity of F = f(ρ). Essentially, we only interested
in the concavity of ρ, which reﬂects the geometry of the space X. However,
due to the linearity of ρ along geodesic segments that realize the distance
between point x and the boundary ∂X, we usually precompose a convex
increasing function f to get the estimate of concavity of F for all directions.
Although any function f satisﬁes (1.1) will work for our estimates, however,
the following choice of f is rather typical:
Proposition 1.2. Let X be a compact n-dimensional Alexandrov space with
nonempty boundary ∂X.
(1) (Theorem 1.8, [AB10]) If curv(x) ≥0 and ∂X is 1-convex in the
Base-Angle sense. Then the function f(ρ(x)) := −(1 −ρ(x))2/2 is
−1-concave.
(2) (Theorem 3.3.1, [Pet07]) If curv(X) ≥1, then f(ρ(x)) := sin(ρ(x))
is −f(ρ)-concave.
For a continuous function φ : [0, a] →R+, we call F is a φ(ρ)-concave
function or the modulus of concavity function of F is φ, if for any t ∈[0, a),
F is φ(t)-concave in the interior of Ωt. One can easily see φ has to be a
nonincreasing function for t ∈[0, a). This is a very special type of con-
cavity, since the concavity depends only on the level-sets of ρ, which makes
the estimates on the gradient curves of diﬀerent parametrizations possible.
Using our language, Proposition 1.2 implies the modulus of concavity for F
is φ(t) = −1 for κ = 0 and φ(t) = −sin(t) for κ = 1.

Abstract: In this note, we estimate the upper bound of volume of closed positively or nonnegatively curved Alexandrov space X with strictly convex boundary. We also discuss the equality case. In par- ticular, the Boundary Conjecture holds when the volume upper bound is achieved. Our theorem also can be applied to Riemannian manifolds with non-smooth boundary, which generalizes Heintze and Karcher’s classical volume comparison theorem. Our main tool is the gradient ﬂow of semi-concave functions. 0. Introduction Let (Mn, g) be a smooth Riemannian manifold and N m ⊂M be a sub- manifold. In [HK78], Heintze and Karcher developed a general comparison theorem for N-Jacobi ﬁelds normal to the submanifold N. As an application, they were able to estimate the volume of a tube around the submanifold N in terms of the lower curvature bound of M and upper bound of the norm of mean curvature vectors of N etc. But the technique does not apply if the embedding N →M is not smooth. For example the boundary of the Alexandrov Lens Sn−2 ∗[0, α] deﬁned in [GMP], with its intrinsic length dis- tance, is a perfectly round sphere Sn−1, but the embedding is non-smooth. To address this kind of problem, we meet non-smooth spaces inevitably. Alexandrov spaces can be viewed as a generalization of Riemannian man- ifolds under lower sectional curvature bound, but with some singularities. Since the spaces that we are interested in are non-smooth in nature, we cannot expect to estimate the whole tube around N without addressing the geometry of the singularities of the embedding N →M. Nevertheless, we are able to estimate the one-side neighborhood of a convex hypersurface. We use [BBI01], [BGP92] and [Pet07] as our references for Alexandrov spaces. We use Alexn(κ) to denote the set of all n-dimensional Alexandrov spaces with lower curvature bound: curv ≥κ. For X ∈Alexn(κ) with ∂X ̸= ∅, the boundary ∂X is geodesically convex by the very deﬁnition of Alexandrov spaces. We need the following deﬁnition from Alexander and Bishop to measure the convexity of ∂X ⊂X quantitatively at footpoints. Recall that p ∈∂X is called a footpoint, if p is the endpoint of a shortest geodesic from a 2000 Mathematics Subject Classiﬁcation. Primary: 53C23.
